title: Which model should you try first?
summary: Choose a tool that can read your input and give you the kind of result you need.

intro.what: One AI can read a movie. Another can study still pictures. Some tools can edit the files in your app. Start with the job you want done.
intro.features: A short trial lets you check speed, cost and results. Keep the same files and rules when you compare tools.
intro.exchange: Use a borderline quota example to compare candidate models.
intro.m365: Score each model on the same meeting note with an unknown owner.
intro.developer: Try the smallest model that passes the exact test your feature needs.
sources: Google · Gemini models and supported media

sections.title: Pick a test with an answer key
paragraphs: Choose a task you can check in a minute. Pick one easy example and one with a catch. These are starting points for your own test.

sections.title: Match the proof to the question
paragraphs: For a rule, you need the exact words and the date. Gemini Notebook can use selected sources. Claude Projects can keep a set of files. ChatGPT can work with files you provide. For a count, you need the rows and the math. “When does the rule start?” calls for a sentence. “How many visits came after that date?” calls for a count you can repeat.

title: Read the price of an AI answer
summary: Learn what a price row means before you compare two bills.

intro.what: An API price tells you what an app pays to send or receive an amount of text. A token is one piece of that text.
intro.features: The table gives sample standard rates. A request can also use thinking tokens or paid tools. A chat subscription has its own rules.
intro.exchange: Count retries when comparing the price of accepted report summaries.
intro.m365: Estimate cost per usable document extraction from the batch totals.
intro.developer: Compare the cost of a successful app response across two trial runs.

sections.title: Read a price row
paragraphs: These base rates are US dollars per million tokens of ordinary text sent in or written back. The two numbers can be different. For 10,000 input tokens, take one hundredth of the input rate. For 2,000 output tokens, take two thousandths of the output rate. Add those two costs. Check discounts, tool fees and the length of your input on the vendor’s price page.

sections.title: Count the wins
paragraphs: Try this pretend game. Model A spends 6 cents to give three useful hints. Model B spends 8 cents to give eight useful hints. Divide each bill by the number of hints that helped. A costs 2 cents per useful hint. B costs 1 cent. Add the cost of bad guesses and repeat tries to find out what the whole job costs.

exercise.prompt: A new run costs 12 cents and gives four useful clues. How much did one useful clue cost?
answer: 12 divided by 4 is 3 cents. Keep a tally of useful clues so you can do the same check on your own runs.
exercise.context: Suppose a game needs helpful clues. Counting the good clues lets you compare two runs even when their prices differ.

title: Make a picture you can actually use
summary: Choose a print, a cut line or a movie, then test the file for that job.

intro.what: A media tool can make a picture, a sound or a clip. The app that uses the result needs a file it can read.
intro.features: An SVG stores drawing shapes. A photo stores dots of color. A movie needs a series of pictures that play in order.
intro.exchange: Check that the legend in a mail-status illustration remains readable.
intro.m365: Inspect an image at its final slide dimensions before placing it.
intro.developer: Verify pixel size, empty margins and legibility for a generated asset.
sources: Adobe · generating video from reference frames

sections.title: Choose a shape or a photo
paragraphs: For a cutout, ask for a single closed outline of a whistle with no words. Open the SVG and check its size. For a print, ask for a photo-style whistle with space for text. For a six-inch by four-inch print at 300 dots per inch, you need 1,800 by 1,200 pixels. Add any exact lettering in a tool where you can edit it.

sections.title: Plan one moving shot
paragraphs: Use a picture of a game token as your starting frame. Ask for one slow camera move while the token stays still. Firefly can use a first frame and, where supported, a last frame. Google and {{model.xai.imagine.name}} have video tools too. Watch the start, middle and end. If the token changes color halfway through, revise that part of the prompt.
sources: Adobe · generating video from reference frames

sections.title: Listen through the real speaker
paragraphs: For narration, give the tool the exact script. For a transcript, give it a recording and check the words. For music, describe the mood and the ending. Try playing a spoken game hint over a short music clip. Listen on your iPad. If a drum hides the score, turn the music down and listen again.

title: Try the same puzzle with three helpers
summary: A made-up parking rule gives you an answer key for a fair test.

intro.what: A fair test gives every helper the same words and the same facts. You decide how to score the answers before you see them.
intro.features: You can repeat a run, change one rule and count what each helper gets right. That is one way to tell whether a change helped.
intro.exchange: Give each helper the same read-only case and record its first answer.
intro.m365: Keep the same input and score sheet when comparing tools on a policy task.
intro.developer: Run identical fee-rule examples before asking any tool to improve its code.

sections.title: Use the same question
paragraphs: Start fresh chats in Gemini, Claude and ChatGPT. Give each this rule: “Charge $2 for each started hour, up to $10 per visit. A visit that starts at 6 p.m. or later costs $4 for the whole visit.” Ask about three visits on one day. A runs from 5:30 p.m. to 7:45 p.m. B runs from 6 p.m. to 6:20 p.m. C runs from 9:05 a.m. to 3:10 p.m. Ask for the charge and the rule used.

sections.title: Score what you can check
paragraphs: Imagine checking a parking receipt before paying. An answer earns credit when the charge agrees with the arrival time and the posted rule.

Give a point for each correct charge. Give one more point if the answer uses the start time for the evening rule. Give one more if it spots the daily limit. A total of five points is possible. Record the time the answer took in a separate box.

rows: It starts before 6 p.m. Two hours and 15 minutes use three started hours.
It starts right at 6 p.m., so the evening rule applies.
Six hours and five minutes use seven started hours. The $14 total stops at the $10 limit.

sections.title: Change just one word
paragraphs: Change “starts” to “ends” in the evening rule. Ask again. A now costs $4 because it ends after 6 p.m. If a helper keeps its old answer, ask it to show the part of the new rule it used. The changed rule tells you more than simply asking the same question again.

title: Four-Tool App Build-Off: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok
summary: Give four builders the same game to make. Play the first files, try one small edit and keep the scores that matter to you.

intro.what: A build-off is a fair tryout. Each tool gets the same request for Harbor Relay Trivia & Scoreboard, a game where two teams share one screen.
intro.features: You get a prompt you can copy, five checks you can repeat and a scorecard for each tool. You can fill them in on this device, even when you read offline.
intro.exchange: Borrow the shared test format to compare mail-report helpers fairly.
intro.m365: Use the same scoring rules when a team compares prototypes.
intro.developer: Play all four original Harbor Relay files and score the same five checks.
sources: OpenAI · ChatGPT Chat, Work and Codex
Claude Help · open and use an Artifact
Gemini Help · build and open an app in Canvas
Grok Bot · find your finished file

buildSpec.prompt: Build a single-file offline web app (`index.html`) for a two-team pass-and-play game called Harbor Relay. Use a clean, bright, high-contrast theme that works on both iPad and desktop screens. Include: (1) Team Blue and Team Gold starting at 0 points, (2) a deck of 6 built-in harbor trivia questions with 3 multiple-choice buttons each, (3) +2 points for a correct answer and 0 points for a wrong answer, automatically switching turns after each answer, (4) a visible Question X of 6 counter and a short explanation after each pick, (5) locking the answer buttons after a pick and after question 6 ends the game, and (6) a Play Again button that resets both scores to 0, resets to Team Blue, and returns to Question 1.
check: Layout & Mobile Fit: All buttons and text fit cleanly on an iPad screen without overlapping or sideways scrolling.
Scoring & Turn Switch: Correct answers add +2 to the active team only; wrong answers add 0; turns alternate Blue -> Gold after every question.
Click-Lock Guard: Tapping an answer twice on the same question cannot award +4 points or skip a turn.
Game End & Winner: After Question 6, answer buttons lock and a clear winner (or tie) banner appears.
Clean Replay: Play Again resets both scores to 0, sets Question 1 of 6, and returns the first turn to Team Blue.
buildSpec.followUp: Change the Play Again button label to New Game. Keep every other word and game rule the same.

sections.title: Set up a fair first try
paragraphs: Make four empty folders, one per tool. Use the same device, browser, screen size and time limit for all four. Pick your time limit before you start. Record the date, mode and model label you actually see.

Start fresh and use the usual settings for each tool. Leave out templates, old files, personal instructions, screenshots and sample code. If a setting is fixed by your account, note that on its card. Keep each tool’s first reply, even if its app fails to open.

sections.title: Play the originals before you open the scorecards
paragraphs: Keep each original as index.html in its own folder. If a reply gives you HTML as text, copy only the code into a plain-text file. If you only get a plan, keep the reply and record that no game ran. Do not ask for a fix during this round.

Test the actual file in a browser with the network off. If tapping HTML in iPad Files only shows a preview, open that file in a browser or viewer that runs local HTML, or test the file on a computer. Use the same iPad screen or browser tablet view for every fit check. Note which you used.

Each game can write its own questions. Learn the answers in a practice round or check the deck in the file. Use the same right-or-wrong pattern in all four games. Count six harbor questions, three choices per question, the number at each turn and one short explanation per pick. Record any missing part in Notes.

First game: Blue answers right on all three turns. Gold misses all three. Double-tap Blue’s first right answer while the first question is still up. Blue should get just 2 and Gold should go next. Finish the game. Blue should win 6 to 0. Try tapping after the end.

Press Play Again. Check for two zeros, Team Blue and Question 1 of 6. Now answer all six correctly. Expect a 6 to 6 tie. To test a Gold win, replay with Gold right on all three turns and Blue wrong on all three.
To test sharing, copy just index.html to a second device by USB or a nearby file transfer. Open it with the internet off and play. If you can test only on one device, write that in Notes.

sections.title: Score the first try, then record your own ratings
paragraphs: A good-looking game can still count the same tap twice. Test the rules first, then record what you liked about using it.

Pick a tool. For each first-try check, select Pass or Fail. Leave checks you have yet to run as Untested. If there was no runnable game, record that in Notes. Distinguish a demonstrated failure from something you could not check.

For the other three rows, use 2 for easy and complete, 1 for partly working or awkward, and 0 if you tried and could not do it. Leave an untried row blank. Score the edit row after the next step. Keep the first five points as their own score.

sections.title: Try exactly one follow-up change
paragraphs: After scoring all four originals, return to each original conversation. Save a spare copy of each file first. Send the same request once. Save each new file in a separate folder and play it again. Look for the new label and check whether the button still resets the game. Keep the first-try scores as recorded.

sections.title: Pick the tool that fits your next build
paragraphs: Choose what matters most for your own project. A reader who makes games may care most about a clear board. Someone making a mail report may care most about rules that work on the first try. A reader who changes a team app often may value quick, clean edits.
Compare the same row across your four cards. If two tools tie there, look at the next thing you care about. A tie is a useful result too. Your scores describe the files, modes and date you tested.
